unit_title: Unit 5: Cultural Heritages - Master Guide on Relative Clauses
content: Unit 5: Grammar Focus - Comprehensive Master Guide on Relative Clauses (Communicative English Skills II - EnLa102) ========================================= 1. CORE CONCEPTS AND FUNDAMENTALS OF RELATIVE CLAUSES ========================================= What is a Relative Clause? A Relative Clause (ደባይ ሀረግ/ዓረፍተ-ነገር) is a subordinate clause that modifies a noun or pronoun in the main clause. It acts like an adjective by giving essential or additional details about a person, object, place, time, or reason. Relative clauses are introduced by either Relative Pronouns or Relative Adverbs: • Relative Pronouns: who, whom, whose, which, that • Relative Adverbs: where, when, why Example: - Direct combination: I saw the girl. She lives near our campus. → I saw the girl who lives near our campus. ========================================= 2. EXHAUSTIVE BREAKDOWN OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS & ADVERBS ========================================= A. Relative Pronouns Matrix (Academic & Exam Standard) 1. WHO (Subject for Persons): • Exclusively refers to human subjects in formal academic grammar. • Subject role: The student who scored highest received an award. 2. WHOM (Object for Persons - Strict Exam Standard): • Exclusively refers to human objects in formal/academic English. • EXAM RULE: For all university exams, always select whom when referring to a person in the object position (e.g., The lecturer whom I met yesterday). • MANDATORY PREPOSITION RULE: Must be used directly after prepositions (e.g., to whom, with whom, about whom, for whom). • Example: Grace is the friend with whom he was in love. 3. WHOSE (Possessive for Persons, Animals, & Objects): • Shows possession or ownership (replaces his, her, its, their). • Example: There is a lucky person whose lottery ticket won 7,000,000 Birr. 4. WHICH (Subject / Object for Animals & Things, or Whole Clauses): • Refers to non-human subjects or objects. • Can also refer back to an entire preceding clause. • Example (Thing): His car, which cost 20,000 pounds, is broken. • Example (Whole clause): She passed me the salt, which fell on the floor. 5. THAT (Subject / Object for Persons, Animals, & Things): • Used ONLY in Defining Relative Clauses. • Replaces who or which in standard restrictive contexts. • STRICT RULE: That can NEVER be used after a comma or after a preposition! • Example: They wanted the picture that cost two pounds. ─────────────────────────── B. Relative Adverbs Matrix 1. WHERE (Place = Preposition + Which): • Modifies places (*in which, at which, on which*). • Example: This is a restaurant where you can find global cuisines. 2. WHEN (Time = Preposition + Which): • Modifies time references (*at which, in which, on which*). • Example: The moment when I found out the exam results was shocking. 3. WHY (Reason = For Which): • Modifies reasons (*for which*). • Example: I would like to know the reason why you decided not to join us. ========================================= 3. DEFINING VS. NON-DEFINING RELATIVE CLAUSES ========================================= A. Defining Relative Clauses (Essential Information) • Function: Contains indispensable information needed to identify the exact noun being discussed. • Commas: NO COMMAS ARE USED. • Use of 'That': That can freely replace who or which. • Omission: The relative pronoun CAN be omitted if it is the object of the clause. - Example 1: The man who sat next to me on the plane talked all the time. (Subject - Cannot omit) - Example 2: This is the shirt (that) I bought. (Object - Pronoun can be omitted: "This is the shirt I bought.") B. Non-Defining Relative Clauses (Extra / Parenthetical Information) • Function: Adds extra, non-essential background details. The main sentence remains complete without it. • Commas: MUST BE ENCLOSED IN COMMAS ( , ... , ). • Use of 'That': 'THAT' IS STRICTLY FORBIDDEN. You must use who, which, whom, or whose. • Omission: The relative pronoun CAN NEVER BE OMITTED. - Example 1: My father, who is 65 now, still works. - Example 2: Los Angeles, which is a popular tourist destination, is a fascinating city. ========================================= 4. OMISSION OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS (ZERO RELATIVE PRONOUN) ========================================= When are you allowed to drop who, whom, which, or that? 1. RULE 1 (Allowed): You can omit the relative pronoun ONLY when it functions as the OBJECT in a defining relative clause. • With Pronoun: The girl whom/that I met yesterday was helpful. • Omitted (Zero Pronoun): The girl [Ø] I met yesterday was helpful. 2. RULE 2 (Not Allowed - Subject Position): If the relative pronoun is the SUBJECT of the verb in the clause, it CANNOT be dropped. • Correct: I saw the girl who was outside our house. • Incorrect: I saw the girl was outside our house. ❌ 3. RULE 3 (Not Allowed - Non-Defining Clauses): You can NEVER drop relative pronouns in non-defining clauses (between commas). ========================================= 5. PITFALL CASES, EXAM TRICKS & COMMON ERRORS (DETAILED ANALYSIS) ========================================= TRICK 1: Using 'That' After a Comma (Non-Defining Trap) ❌ INCORRECT: Gondar, that is famous for its castles, is located in northern Ethiopia. ✅ CORRECT: Gondar, which is famous for its castles, is located in northern Ethiopia. • Detailed Underlying Grammar Rule: Non-defining relative clauses provide parenthetical, extra details about a noun that is already fully identified (*Gondar*). In formal English syntax, the relative complementizer that is strictly restricted to defining (restrictive) clauses. Because commas visually and grammatically isolate non-defining clauses, placing that after a comma violates this core rule. • Exam Application: Always inspect the punctuation preceding the target gap. If a comma is present immediately before the blank space, eliminate that instantly. Choose which for non-human antecedents and who/whom for human antecedents. TRICK 2: Preposition + 'That' or 'Who' Trap ❌ INCORRECT: The scholar to who I spoke yesterday gave a lecture. ❌ INCORRECT: The book about that we talked is in the library. ✅ CORRECT: The scholar to whom I spoke yesterday gave a lecture. ✅ CORRECT: The book about which we talked is in the library. • Detailed Underlying Grammar Rule: Prepositions in formal English must govern pronouns in their objective grammatical case. The subjective pronoun who cannot directly follow a preposition; it must take the formal objective form whom. Furthermore, the relative pronoun that cannot tolerate fronted prepositions (*to that*, *about that*). If a preposition is placed at the front of the clause, that is completely invalidated. • Exam Application: When you observe a preposition (to, with, about, in, for, of, on, by) standing right before the blank, narrow your choices down strictly to whom (for persons) or which (for non-persons). Forms like *to who*, *about that*, or *with that* are immediate distractor options. TRICK 3: Human Object Trap ('Who' vs. 'Whom') ❌ INCORRECT (In Formal Exams): The candidate who we interviewed yesterday was selected. ✅ CORRECT (Formal Exam Standard): The candidate whom we interviewed yesterday was selected. • Detailed Underlying Grammar Rule: Relative pronouns maintain case roles (Subject vs. Object) relative to the verb inside the clause. In the relative clause "we interviewed yesterday", the subject is already present (*we*), and the action (*interviewed*) is directed at the candidate. Thus, the candidate acts as the syntactic direct object. In standardized university examinations, object positions referring to humans must strictly take whom, whereas who is reserved solely for subject positions. • Exam Application: Conduct the He/Him Test on the clause: rephrase the clause as an independent sentence (*"We interviewed him/her"*). If the objective pronoun (*him/her/them*) fits, the test proves you need whom in your exam choice. TRICK 4: The Double Pronoun / Resumptive Pronoun Trap ❌ INCORRECT: The cultural heritage that we preserved it last year is valuable. ✅ CORRECT: The cultural heritage that we preserved last year is valuable. • Detailed Underlying Grammar Rule: Relative pronouns (`that`, `which`, `who`, `whom`) act as substitute terms that front the clause while replacing the original noun/pronoun. When you insert a relative pronoun like that or which, it already fills the grammatical role of direct object within the clause. Retaining the personal pronoun (*it*, *him*, *her*, *them*) inside the clause creates an illegal grammatical redundancy known as a "resumptive pronoun". • Exam Application: Scan the rest of the relative clause following the relative pronoun. If you see a personal object pronoun (*it*, *them*, *him*, *her*) referring back to the main noun, strike that option out immediately. TRICK 5: 'Where' vs. 'Which' for Places Trap ❌ INCORRECT: This is the historical monument where I visited last week. ✅ CORRECT: This is the historical monument which/that I visited last week. ✅ CORRECT: This is the historical monument where I stayed last week. • Detailed Underlying Grammar Rule: The relative adverb where replaces a spatial prepositional phrase (*in which*, *at which*, *on which*). It requires the verb inside the relative clause to be an intransitive location verb or a verb followed by a prepositional complement (e.g., *stayed at*, *lived in*). However, transitive verbs like *visit*, *renovate*, *buy*, *build*, or *see* directly govern the place noun as a direct object without any preposition. Therefore, direct objects must take the relative pronouns which or that, never where. • Exam Application: Apply the Preposition Test: try adding a preposition to the end of the clause. *"I visited AT the monument"* is incorrect English, so where cannot be used (use *which/that*). *"I stayed AT the monument"* is correct English, so where (or *at which*) is required. TRICK 6: 'Whose' vs. 'Who's' Contraction Trap ❌ INCORRECT: The researcher who's manuscript was published gave a lecture. ✅ CORRECT: The researcher whose manuscript was published gave a lecture. • Detailed Underlying Grammar Rule: Despite sounding identical in speech, whose and who's belong to completely different syntactic classes. Whose is a possessive relative determiner indicating ownership or association between two nouns (*researcher's manuscript*). On the other hand, who's is purely a phonetic contraction representing either *who is* or *who has*. • Exam Application: Use the Expansion Test whenever you see *who's* as an option. Expand *who's* into *who is* or *who has* in the sentence (*"The researcher who is manuscript..."*). If the expansion results in grammatical nonsense, select the possessive form whose. ─────────────────────────── SPECIAL PITFALL TRICK QUESTIONS (EXHAUSTIVE EXAM EXPLANATIONS): Pitfall Question 1 (Quantifier + Preposition Trap): The university hired thirty new instructors, many of ________ hold doctorate degrees. A. who B. whom C. that D. whose • Correct Answer: B. whom • Detailed Rationale & Mechanism: Quantifying expressions like many of, all of, some of, neither of, none of, two of end with the preposition of. According to formal preposition rules (Trick 2), any human pronoun directly governed by a preposition must take the formal objective form whom. Options A (*who*) and C (*that*) are grammatically forbidden after prepositions. Option D (*whose*) is incorrect because no possessed noun follows the blank. Pitfall Question 2 (Nominal Relative Pronoun Trap - 'What' vs 'Which'): She did not agree with ________ the guest speaker stated during the presentation. A. which B. that C. what D. in which • Correct Answer: C. what • Detailed Rationale & Mechanism: Standard relative pronouns (*which*, *that*, *who*) require an explicit antecedent noun occurring immediately before them in the main clause. In this sentence, there is no noun antecedent preceding the gap—only the preposition *with*. The nominal relative pronoun what inherently contains its own antecedent (*what* = *the thing(s) that*). Therefore, when no antecedent noun exists to modify, what must be selected. Pitfall Question 3 (Clause-Modifying 'Which' Trap): He scored full marks in all five freshman modules, ________ surprised all his instructors. A. that B. what C. which D. this • Correct Answer: C. which • Detailed Rationale & Mechanism: While most relative pronouns refer to a single preceding noun, which possesses a unique grammatical function: it can modify an ENTIRE prior proposition (*scoring full marks in all five modules*). Because this whole situation is an extra non-defining observation set off by a comma, only which can function as the sentential relative pronoun. Option A (*that*) is disqualified by the comma, Option B (*what*) cannot modify prior sentences, and Option D (*this*) would create an illegal comma splice. Pitfall Question 4 (Stranded Preposition & Object Repetition Trap): That is the senior researcher whom I was speaking ________. A. about him B. about C. about which D. about that • Correct Answer: B. about • Detailed Rationale & Mechanism: The relative pronoun whom has already been placed at the front of the clause to act as the object of the preposition. The preposition about belongs at the end of the verb phrase (*stranded preposition*). Option A (*about him*) introduces an illegal resumptive pronoun (*him*). Option C (*about which*) incorrectly repeats the preposition while using a non-human pronoun for a human researcher. Option D (*about that*) incorrectly duplicates the preposition and attempts to place *that* after it.
